Chapter Two: The Strange Logic of Grief and the Persistence of Magical Thinking.
When someone you love is suddenly gone, your mind becomes this strange place where reality and hope keep wrestling with each other. Part of you knows the truth—really knows it, deep down. But there’s another part that just can’t accept it, that desperately hopes maybe, somehow, they’ll walk back through the door. That’s what we call magical thinking. It’s where logic and longing get all tangled up.
Suddenly, everyday things feel different. That old pair of shoes by the door? They’re not just shoes anymore—they’re a sign, a tiny hope that maybe their owner will need them again. And you might leave a favorite chair untouched, almost like you’re saving their spot, just in case. You find yourself acting out little rituals, or avoiding certain things, or replaying conversations in your mind, hoping—just maybe—you could change what happened. It doesn’t make sense, but honestly, it’s one of the most human things we do.
Most people think grief has a tidy order: first shock, then denial, then anger, and finally, acceptance. But real grief? It’s a lot messier than that. Your mind keeps circling back, reliving the moment of loss, searching for some way to undo it. It’s almost like, if you could just think the right thought or do the right thing, maybe the past could change. You’re not choosing this—it just happens, like an instinct when everything feels too much.
You start obsessing over every detail. The medical reports, the timelines, the last conversation you had. There’s this deep need to understand, to find a reason, as if it might give you back some control. Sometimes that search is comforting. Other times, it’s tormenting, a stark reminder of how random and unfair tragedy can be.
Meanwhile, the world outside keeps spinning. Friends offer their sympathy, but their lives just keep moving forward. And you? You feel cut off, almost invisible—like you’re stuck in a different reality where time moves at a completely different pace.
Your mind doesn’t want closure, not really. It holds on to hope, no matter how irrational. Deep down, you wish for some loophole in the universe—a way the rules might bend, and you could have a reunion. That’s magical thinking. It’s not logical, but it’s a way to survive the unthinkable.
Little by little, you start to notice what’s happening. You realize your mind’s playing tricks, that these rituals and obsessions are just ways of coping. But recognizing that doesn’t make it stop. Sometimes, the need for hope—even if it doesn’t make sense—is stronger than the need for the truth.
So many of us fall into these patterns, finding comfort in routines, even when they don’t add up anymore. The daily habits become a lifeline, a way to stay connected to what’s been lost. You move through the world feeling half here, half somewhere else—caught between memory and reality.
And eventually, it becomes clear: grief isn’t really about letting go. It’s about learning to live with the absence. The person you lost? They’re never fully gone. They’re there in your thoughts, your heart, and in all the tiny details of daily life. Grief is about finding your way through this new reality, looking for meaning, even when everything feels chaotic.
